WBPH033-10.title: Electricity and Magnetism
WBPH033-10.priorKnowledge:
The course assumes prior knowledge of calculus and classical physics acquired in the first semester: Mechanics and Relativity (WBPH001-10), Calculus I (WBPH057-05), Calculus II (WBPH058-05), or equivalents elsewhere.

In particular, students should be familiar with classical and relativistic mechanics, vector algebra (curvilinear coordinate systems, volume elements), complex numbers, and differential and integral vector calculus (divergence, gradient, and curl theorems).

WBPH072-05.title: Physics Lab: Advanced Applications 1
WBPH072-05.priorKnowledge: This course builds on knowledge gained in the two first-year courses: Physics Lab: Skills (WBPH077-05) and Physics Lab: Design Project (WBPH075-05). In the second course, students learn how to carry out a complete small-scale project in a team, including 3D design. Teamwork is an essential component of the second course.

WMBE024-05.title: Control Engineering for BME
WMBE024-05.priorKnowledge:
Required is a background accquired from the following Bachelor's courses:
- Linear Algebra (for BME): linear matrix equations, vector spaces, eigenvalues & eigenvectors
- Calculus 1 (for BME): differentiation, integration, Taylor polynomial, complex numbers

sourceUse: The TER index and internal headings identify the 2026–2027 appendix despite legacy PDF metadata. The standard major and its deepening minor are one programme, with 60 EC each year. The TER and dated course entry use Differential Equations; the older Mathematical Physics name survives in the public overview and some course descriptions. The appendix is controlling.

Normally requires 150 EC in Applied Physics. Third-year students who earn at least 135 EC within their first three years of registration may also start. Students complete an individual project, report and presentation.

progression.firstYear: Calculus 2 and Differential Equations build on Calculus 1. Electricity and Magnetism builds on first-semester mechanics and calculus. Physics Lab: Design Project expects the first lab and physics knowledge; Electricity and Magnetism spans the same semester with the design lab in block 2b. The catalogue describes prior knowledge and does not list a separate formal completion gate for that concurrent course.
progression.secondYear: Computational Methods 2 draws on first-year mathematics, mechanics, electromagnetism and lab work. Waves and Optics uses calculus, linear algebra and electromagnetism. Quantum Physics 1 precedes From Atoms to Solids. The advanced applications labs use the earlier lab sequence.
progression.thirdYear: Control Engineering lists mathematics, signals, electronics and mechanics as background. The required Applied Physics courses supply corresponding mathematics, differential equations, signal processing, electronics and mechanics. BME course examples describe expected content rather than a separate degree-specific enrollment requirement. Device Physics draws on solid-state foundations; Solid State Physics is in block 1a before Device Physics in block 1b.
progression.restrictedChoices: The first listed option from each group is illustrated neutrally. Atoms and Molecules in 1a draws on year-two quantum and waves. Measurement Systems in 1b uses earlier electromagnetism, electronics and lab uncertainty. Nanoprobing and Nanofabrication in 2a draws on prior solid-state physics. Its catalogue note about Nanoscience and Nanotechnology refers to Physics NExT and Energy and Environment tracks; the Applied Physics TER explicitly includes it as an eligible choice. The selected route does not duplicate Tailored Project across groups.
progression.research: The dated course page describes individual research with a supervisor, report and symposium. The TER permits 150 EC normally or 135 EC for third-year students within their first three years of registration. The illustrated sequence reaches 150 EC after year-three autumn and 165 EC before the research project begins in spring block 2b.
